title: First Grade Worksheets: Free Printable Maths Worksheets + Quiz
meta_title: Free Printable First Grade Worksheets (Maths) + Quiz
meta_desc: What free printable first grade maths worksheets should cover, how to pick good ones, and a print-and-practise routine that sticks, plus a free quiz.
excerpt: A stack of free printable first grade worksheets is only useful if you print the right ones and use them well. Here is what to look for, a weekly routine, and a quick quiz to check where your child stands.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Type ‘free printable first grade worksheets’ into any search box and you will drown in results — hundreds of PDFs, half of them American, a good number riddled with clip-art and almost no actual practice. I have watched parents in Tier-2 cities print forty pages in an evening, hand them to a six-year-old, and wonder a week later why nothing stuck. The problem is rarely the child. It is that a pile of random sheets is not a plan.

Free printables are genuinely useful — you can print the same page ten times, there is no screen, and a child gets to hold a pencil. But they only work if you pick the right ones and use them with a bit of structure. Here is how I would go about it.

What free printable first grade worksheets should cover

Grade 1 maths in India follows the NCERT flow, and a good set of worksheets should mirror it rather than jump around. Over a year, your printables should touch every one of these strands:

  • Numbers to 100 — counting, reading, writing, and ordering, plus what comes before, after and between.
  • Addition and subtraction within 20 — the bulk of the year’s arithmetic, moving from pictures to number sentences.
  • Place value — tens and ones, the idea that 34 means 3 tens and 4 ones.
  • Shapes — 2D and 3D, sorting by sides and corners.
  • Measurement — long and short, heavy and light, full and empty.
  • Money, time and patterns — recognising coins, telling time to the hour, extending simple patterns.

If a free bundle only ever gives you ‘add two single digits’ on every page, it is not a Grade 1 syllabus — it is one topic wearing forty different costumes.

How to pick a good free printable

Not all free sheets are equal, and the bad ones quietly teach bad habits. Before you print, run each worksheet past this quick checklist:

  • Is there an answer key? A worksheet with no answers puts you on the hook to solve every question, and you will skip it. This is the single most common failing of free PDFs.
  • Is the print density right? Around 8 to 12 questions per page. A wall of 40 sums intimidates a six-year-old; four questions with a cartoon border teach nothing.
  • Does it use Indian context? Rupees, not dollars. Names like Aarav and Meera. It matters more than you would think for a child making sense of a word problem.
  • Is it black-and-white friendly? Heavy colour backgrounds drain a cartridge and print as grey mud. Line-art prints cleanly and cheaply.
  • Does it build, page to page? Sheet 2 should be a small step past sheet 1, not a random new topic.

Free printables vs a structured workbook

Free sheets and a paid workbook are not rivals — they do different jobs. This is roughly how I weigh them for a Grade 1 parent:

What you needFree printablesStructured workbook
CostFreeSmall one-time cost
Answer keysHit or missAlways included
Follows NCERT orderRarelyYes, chapter by chapter
Difficulty builds upYou sequence itAlready graded
Best forExtra drill on one weak topicThe whole year’s practice

My honest take: use free printables to hammer a specific weak spot — say your child keeps tripping on making ten — and lean on one graded workbook for the steady, everyday practice that follows the syllabus in order.

A print-and-practise routine that sticks

Ten focused minutes a day beats an hour once a week, every single time. Here is a five-day rhythm parents I know have made work without tears:

  • Monday and Tuesday: one number or place-value sheet — the foundation everything else sits on.
  • Wednesday and Thursday: addition or subtraction within 20, the year’s heavy lifting.
  • Friday: a mixed sheet — shapes, money, or time — so it never gets stale.

Two rules make the difference. First, sit with your child for the first two questions, then step back and let them finish alone; the goal is independence, not supervision. Second, mark it together the same day using the answer key, and re-do only the ones they got wrong. A worksheet you never check is a worksheet you may as well not have printed.

Print smart, not often

Print single-sided so there is room to work, keep a cheap folder so completed sheets pile up as visible proof of progress, and print the same tricky page twice a week apart rather than a fresh topic every day. Repetition on a hard idea is not boring for a six-year-old — it is how the idea finally clicks.

The mistake most parents make

The trap is treating volume as progress. Forty finished pages feel productive, but if none were checked and none were re-done, the child has practised their mistakes into permanence. Fewer sheets, marked properly and revisited, beat a thick stack that nobody ever corrected. Slow is smooth, and smooth is fast.

Try the quiz, then print with a plan

Before you print anything, the short free quiz below tells you where your child actually stands across Grade 1 maths — numbers, addition, place value and shapes. Let them try it, read the explanations together for anything they miss, and then choose worksheets that target the gaps. When you want a full year of graded, NCERT-aligned practice with answer keys already done for you, the printable workbook linked below saves you the hunt.

quiz.title: First Grade Maths Check Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions across Grade 1 maths — numbers, addition, subtraction, place value and shapes. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Counting up by one from 49 gives 50.
Make ten: take 3 from the 6 to turn 7 into 10, then add the leftover 3. 10 + 3 = 13.

questions.q: In the number 34, how many tens are there?
questions.explanation: 34 means 3 tens and 4 ones, so there are 3 tens.
A triangle has exactly 3 sides and 3 corners.

questions.q: Which coin is worth the most?
questions.explanation: Of these, the ₹5 coin has the highest value.

questions.q: What comes next in the pattern: 2, 4, 6, __?
questions.explanation: The pattern goes up by 2 each time, so after 6 comes 8.

questions.q: A clock shows the hour hand on 3 and the minute hand on 12. What time is it?
questions.explanation: When the minute hand points to 12 and the hour hand to 3, it is 3 o’clock.

faq.q: Are free printable worksheets enough for Grade 1 maths?
faq.a: For extra practice on a specific weak topic, yes. For the whole year, free sheets often skip the NCERT order and rarely include answer keys, so most parents pair them with one graded workbook that covers the full syllabus.

faq.q: How many worksheets should a first grader do in a day?
faq.a: One sheet of about 8 to 12 questions, roughly ten focused minutes. Marking it and re-doing the wrong ones matters far more than the number of pages finished.

faq.q: What maths topics should first grade worksheets cover?
faq.a: Numbers to 100, addition and subtraction within 20, place value (tens and ones), 2D and 3D shapes, measurement, money, time to the hour, and simple patterns — matching the NCERT Grade 1 flow.

faq.q: How do I use printable worksheets without a printer at home?
faq.a: Save the PDFs to a phone or pen drive and print a week’s worth at a local shop for a few rupees, or work through them on a tablet in a PDF app and copy answers into a notebook.
